questions.q: What kinds of events does the default trace capture?
options: Database file auto-growth/auto-shrink, database and object creation/deletion, and some security-related events
Every row-level data modification made by any user
questions.explain: The default trace is a lightweight, always-on trace capturing a fixed set of server-level events useful for after-the-fact diagnosis.

questions.q: How would you find whether the default trace is running and its file location?
questions.explain: sys.traces with is_default = 1 identifies the default trace and its current file, which sys.fn_trace_gettable can then read.

options: Closes the current error log file and starts a new one, without restarting the instance
Deletes all historical error log files immediately
questions.explain: This lets a DBA start a fresh, manageable error log file periodically on a server that stays up for months without needing a restart.

questions.q: By default, when does SQL Server create a new error log file?
options: Only when manually requested via sp_configure
Never — there is only ever one error log file
questions.explain: A new error log file is created on every restart, which is why a server that rarely restarts can accumulate one very large, hard-to-search log.

questions.q: Why is priority boost described as a discouraged legacy option?
options: It raised SQL Server's OS scheduling priority and could starve the OS and other processes
It was required for Always On Availability Groups to function
It doubled the maximum number of user connections
questions.explain: priority boost is deprecated/removed in current versions; Microsoft discouraged it even while it existed because of its risk to overall system stability.
